title: Go SDK stream-multiplex: per-request timeboxing and adaptive preemption
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Problem: Long-lived multiplexed streaming connections occasionally allow low-priority requests to occupy the shared runtime and KV cache beyond their useful deadline, causing higher-priority short requests to see increased tail latency and SLO violations. Goal: implement per-request timeboxing and an adaptive preemption policy in the Go SDK runtime to ensure high-priority requests are served with predictable latency while preserving throughput for background work.
background: Existing work focuses on cooperative cancellation and deadline propagation across streaming RPCs, but we observed two concrete operational patterns: 1) multi-message background sends that hold the stream open for seconds (e.g., bulk reranking), 2) client-side prefetch that continues after a faster interactive query arrives over the same multiplexed connection. Both patterns lead to blocking on per-connection resources (KV caches, kernel scheduling slots). Current SDK contracts allow cancellation but don't provide a lightweight preemption primitive or explicit timebox at the request boundary.
proposal_summary: Add a per-request Timebox parameter to stream requests exposed in the Go SDK API. Internally, the stream multiplexer will track per-request progress and, when the connection is under contention or a higher-priority request arrives, will attempt a best-effort preemption sequence: signal to the server with an Out-of-band PREEMPT frame (if supported by server/runtime), gracefully checkpoint partial work to KV cache, and close the outstanding request with a canonical error (StreamPreempted). If the server/runtime cannot honor PREEMPT, fall back to a local cooperative cancellation trigger that races with request processing. Provide adaptive heuristics tuned by observed request durations and SLO targets.
acceptance_criteria: Go SDK API exposes Timebox() on stream request builder with default unset
When Timebox expires, request is terminated with canonical error StreamTimeboxed and SDK surfaces clear retryable vs non-retryable guidance
Under simulated contention, high-priority requests see 99th percentile latency improvement >= 30% compared to baseline
End-to-end e2e tests that validate PREEMPT frame path and cooperative cancel fallback
Design doc reviewed by runtime and infra teams and feature flags gated for controlled rollout
design_notes: API ergonomics: prefer functional option pattern: client.Stream(ctx, WithTimebox(200*time.Millisecond), WithPriority(High))
Server signal: runtime will accept a lightweight PREEMPT message; spec proposal at https://governance.internal/redwood/preempt-spec (design artifact)
Fallback: cooperative cancellation via existing context cancel; this ensures behavior on legacy runtime remains correct
Metrics: instrument preempt_attempts, preempt_success, timeboxed_count, timeboxed_latency_histogram, and per-priority tail latencies
SLO impact: add SLIs that measure tail latency for priority=High; default Timebox must not break normal batch workloads
tradeoffs: Pro: predictable low-latency for interactive flows; limits noisy neighbors on shared connections
Con: added complexity in multiplexer and risk of partial-result semantics; need clear docs for application developers
Conservative rollout reduces client-side surprises: feature flag + opt-in Timebox and Priority enums
Requires runtime support for PREEMPT to be fully graceful; without PREEMPT, behavior relies on best-effort cancellation and may abort work mid-stream
implementation_steps: 1) Introduce Timebox and Priority options in Go SDK stream API (client-go v0.X)
2) Add multiplexer tracking for per-request wall-time and progress checkpoints
3) Implement PreemptCoordinator that issues PREEMPT frames or falls back to context cancel
4) Add canonical errors: StreamPreempted, StreamTimeboxed, and retryability annotations
5) Add unit tests for API surfaces and multiplexer logic
6) End-to-end test harness: local runtime stub that supports PREEMPT and a legacy stub without PREEMPT
7) Feature flag rollout: internal canary -> staged customers -> default off for GA
8) Docs: SDK README examples, migration guide, and best-practice patterns for batch vs interactive workloads
9) Post-rollout: collect metrics and tune adaptive heuristics for default Timebox and preemption thresholds
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: unexpected application errors when mid-stream work is preempted. Mitigation: canonical errors with clear retry semantics and example patterns for checkpointing state.
Risk: false positives (preempting work that was almost done). Mitigation: adaptive heuristics that look at percent-complete and favor finishing work under low remaining time cost.
Risk: additional resource churn from frequent preemption under high load. Mitigation: backoff controls and rate-limit preemptions per connection.
Risk: runtime upgrade mismatch. Mitigation: cooperative cancel fallback ensures correctness across mixed-version fleets and SDK can expose config to disable PREEMPT if runtime lacks support.
progress_updates: 2025-02-15: Spike completed — prototype multiplexer tracked per-request timestamps and could cancel via context; microbenchmarks show 20% 99p improvement in simple contended scenario
2025-02-20: Design doc posted for review at https://confluence.redwood/internal/go-sdk-stream-preempt; requested feedback from runtime and infra
2025-02-24: API shape agreed in design review; opted for WithTimebox(duration) functional option and Priority enum (Low/Normal/High/Background)
2025-03-01: Implemented initial PreemptCoordinator and added canonical errors; unit tests green locally
2025-03-03: Opened RFC PR for PREEMPT wire frame spec and runtime shim: https://github.com/redwood/repro/rfcs/pull/54
open_questions: Should Timebox semantics be absolute (from request start) or sliding (from last activity)? Current plan uses absolute wall-time but open to sliding window for streaming producers.
What should be the default Timebox for interactive endpoints exposed by the hosted API? Ops prefers conservative 300ms; product prefers 150ms for aggressive interactivity.
How to expose checkpointing hooks in the SDK so application authors can implement efficient resumable background work? Proposal: optional OnCheckpoint callback on the stream request builder.
Rate limiting preemption: what is acceptable default for per-connection preempt_attempts per minute?
rollout_plan: Phase 0: internal build and unit/e2e tests behind feature flag (sdk.flag.preempt=false)
Phase 1: Canary with internal services that opt-in (monitor preempt_success rate and tail latency improvements)
Phase 2: Gradual opt-in for selected external customers and documentation package
Phase 3: Default SDK enabled with conservative adaptive heuristics and telemetry collection for 4 weeks before GA
testing_plan: Unit tests for Timebox edge cases and canonical error mapping
Integration tests: legacy-runtime and preempt-capable runtime behaviour
Load tests with synthetic mix (90% background long streams, 10% interactive) to validate tail latency improvements
Chaos test: simulate PREEMPT message losses and validate fallback cancellation correctness
next_steps: Address open questions from runtime team and finalize PREEMPT wireframe RFC
Complete checkout hooks for OnCheckpoint and add example in examples/streaming/preempt-resume.go
Add observability dashboards for preemption metrics and per-priority latency slices
Schedule follow-up design review with product to agree on sensible defaults and messaging
